decision.audit_notes: The same-session $25,000 offer supersedes her earlier pass for the pitch-window label.

turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
From Gimlet, this is The Pitch. I’m Josh Muccio
On this show, we venture into the world of startups, to a critical moment, when aspiring entrepreneurs put it all on the line and pitch investors for funding.
This week…

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: We produce wearable technology and we allow people to play combat sports without having to hit each other in the face.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Phil, you're a moron. I have to tell you. And I never say that...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Did you just call me a moron?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text:
Yeah, I did.
Today, two founders pitch their wearable fitness technology -- basically a Fitbit for boxing. Will investors decide that their device is a heavyweight?
Phil Nadel is the founder of Forefront Venture Partners. In pitches, you’ll hear him put the focus on the hard numbers.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text:
I don't like the model. I'm not seeing the path to recurring revenue.
Jillian Manus is here representing Structure Capital. She tends to only go in on companies when she really understands -- and appreciates -- what they’re doing.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text:
I see the merit. I just want to make sure I always add smart money, just not money.
Jake Chapman’s here with Gelt VC. He looks for founders who have thought through all the small, boring details..

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text:
There are a ton, a ton of operational issues that you haven't had to address yet. I think you can address these issues, but we haven't seen that yet.
Howie Diamond founded the VC firm, Ranch Ventures. He looks for scrappy founders who, come hell or high water, get the job done.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text:
It's just one of my things, as an investor. I want to know that you can build something that's actually functional.
Here we go.

turns.speaker: Khalil Zahar
turns.text:
Let’s jump into it, I think its a good time. Thanks a lot for having us, guys. My name is Khalil. I'm the founder of our company that is called Hykso. We produce wearable technology and we allow people to play combat sports without having to hit each other in the face.
Basically, Hykso is a chip you can wear on your wrist, sort of like a Fitbit. But instead of measuring steps or how many flights of stairs you've climbed, it counts punches. How many punches you've thrown, what kind of punches, and how fast they were. So if you were taking, for instance, a kickboxing class, you could see how you were measuring up.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text:
Uh, but we realized that a lot of coaches out there are trying to always gamify those classes, and trying to keep score basically, and they have no way to do it. And right now, the best thing available is a company called MYZONE, which is actually a heart rate monitor that displays the heart rate directly on TV.
Here is Tommy, the other founder.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text:
Heart rate is a very tough way to measure output, first of all. Because it's subject to so many external factors, whether it be stress or caffeine.
Tommy’s the muscle in this co-founding team. No, literally. His hands are wrapped like he's ready to step into the ring. And on his wrists, hidden under the wrap, sits the technology that brings everyone in here today.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: And the competition aspect is really what excites us. Because you can now create a circuit and connect all of those locations together, within gyms for example.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I guess I'm having trouble. Can you guys just very concisely tell me where this company started, where it is today, where you see it in the future, and what's actually built up to now. That would be helpful.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text:
It started three years ago. And the idea was just for myself. And then we had a lot of traction with the professional athletes. Because we were working with the national team of Canada, they needed very high accuracy. And basically, what took the most of our time to develop this, is that you have to filter all the different types of data. If you do jumping jacks, you don't want to count punches. If you clap your hands, you don't want to count punches. And that was a very big challenge.
Khalil and Tommy explain that because they started out working with the Canadian Olympic Boxing team, the process of refining their wearable technology took a while. They needed it to be precise in measuring punches -- and punches only. But finally, they got it right… and it was then that they decided to take their product to a bigger market.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Target demographic is boxers and boxing gyms today?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: No, it's actually wider than that. Right now, the target market when it comes to the users, is actually women between 25 and 40 years old. They're the big market when it comes to fitness. We’re marketing to them through the gyms.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text:
It was a pivot, to go to the gym model. It just makes a lot more sense for us.
Rather than marketing to individual consumers -- or to teams like the Canadian Boxing team-- the new plan for Hykso is to sell directly to
gyms.
This way athletes taking classes like kickboxing and MMA can all use the wearables and keep track of their progress.
The question is -- how well does the technology actually work?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: You guys wanna see a demo?

turns.speaker: Investors
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: I wanna show you a demo, too. I'm dying. Do you want to hold the phone for them?

turns.text: Show them that, too.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Take it easy. Not the face.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: It would have been Sheel, but...

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: This is the moneymaker right here.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text:
The sensor's right here. He's holding the charging dock. Both sensors go within that charging dock. It doubles as a carrying case for you.
Tommy is showing the investors the sensor, which sits inside the wrap that goes underneath his boxing glove.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: So punch harder, punch faster, punch more, you maximize that intensity score. So I throw a punch - how many punches am I at right now Khalil?

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text:
13, 14, 15, 16, 17.
Tommy is throwing punches now, showing investors how the Hykso sensor can pick up the speed, velocity, and type of each punch.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So we need a little more velocity. Come on man.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: I'm retired.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Let's get it over 12.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Oh intensity through the roof.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Off the charts.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: See, see what the social pressure does. Imagine in a gym setting, right, when your stats are up on a TV screen?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Oh right, you're off the charts.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: The instructor's like, pick it up! Pick it up Jake!

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: So imagine you're in a gym setting now, right. And individual you have that social pressure. The other modes we have are super interesting too. So imagine you can take the gym now, and you split the class into two teams or four teams of equal size. And now you have team one, team two, team three, team four coming together to beat one another.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And you can tally it by team?

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text:
The 6:00 class coming together to beat the 8:00 class. Because in a gym, and I spent a really long time in fitness myself, the holy grail in a gym is community. If you can get that community feel in your gym, strengthen those relationships, you drive retention through the roof.
As a rule, investors love seeing a live demo -- and they view it as kind of a first hurdle: if the founders can nail the demo, then they’ll move on to the tough questions.

turns.text: Could not any of the other Fitbit or wearable companies come out with this?

turns.text: Yeah, but Apple's also working on things. They're all, I'm not just saying Fitbit, I'm saying wearables in general, as a category.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: So what we do is full 3D motion tracking. The sensor knows its position in time and space 1000 times per second.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right, but it can be done by any one of the wearable companies?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: Right. And honestly when it comes to the Fitbit, the angle of the product is completely different.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But she used that as an example.

turns.speaker: Jillian

turns.text: Let's say I started Phil's Boxing Sensor company and I did the same training machine learning. What's proprietary?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: What is proprietary is actually the algorithms. It's hard to know if there's not other brands out there who can do that. We know HBO worked for two years on a similar product and wasn't able to pull it off.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Are you thinking of doing like a Peloton for boxing?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text:
Yes. Exactly. At a certain point, we want to allow people even at home to connect with the people in the gym.

It's a $1200 stationary bike that comes with a big screen, and you ride it in your home. They have a $50 monthly membership that lets you tune into live classes.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: To me that makes a lot more sense than even having to go to the gym. I'll stay at home like I do with my Peloton, and I'll go online and do an interactive class or compete with other boxers.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: Yep. Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That's smart. I really like that idea. Because, well, firstly Peloton is killing it. And with your model they don't have to buy expensive hardware. turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: And not just that, but I think the at-home fitness market has always been more geared towards women. Women have been more accepting as an overall of the at-home fitness market. And it's obviously a huge opportunity right now.

turns.speaker: Tommy
turns.text: No.

turns.text: It's because Jane Fonda.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: Tae Bo was another one.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: For the record, I had a jazzercise party when I was three. So I was into it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Did you have a jazzercise!

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I can see that.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text:
My opinion of you has changed dramatically now.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So how does this fit into that model? Because you don't have really the workouts, do you? It's just the device right now, just the sensor.

turns.text: Is the sensors?

turns.text: Which one?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: It's called Title Boxing Club.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text:
Oh yeah. I know that.

Title Boxing Club recently signed a Letter of Intent -- an LOI -- basically saying that if Hykso builds the sensors and leaderboard app for the gyms, they will buy it.

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text: They're expanding super-fast right now. And they basically were looking into MYZONE, but they didn't like the fact that it was irrelevant for boxing. turns.text: What do you think the value of that LOI is?

turns.speaker: Khalil
turns.text:
$2 million.
LOIs worth two million dollars is nothing to sniff at -- though it’s worth distinguishing that LOIs are
not
contracts. Still, they could turn into contracts if everything goes right for Hykso.
The question on all the investors’ minds now is: assuming this does work, how big could Hykso really get?

turns.text: Do you think this is going to be a trend? Is this trend sensitive?

turns.text: You know, it's hard to say. You know, I don't believe so. Spinning has not been a trend, although it started...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Actually, that's a really good question. I'm thinking more like a fad.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: A fad fades quickly.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, now, Tae Bo was everything, and now it's gone. Everything comes and goes.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Howie, what about jazzercise? Has that gone? How's that going for you?

And then in 2015, there's like multiple analysts in fitness that are saying that combat sport is the new thing.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But I'm wondering if it's a new fad, where this has only a little bit, it's going to peak similarly and then that's it.

turns.text: Basically when we learned that the sale cycles were so long, and that was last January, we decided to do a pre-order campaign. That was in March, and in 4 months we sold 2500 units. It's $360,000.
